$comment: The account-scope finding inventory: every finding harness/account_scope_check.py can report, the severity it is reported at, and the exact command or edit that fixes it. The set of ids here is asserted equal to FINDINGS in that module by core's suite -- in BOTH directions, for tenancy_findings.json's reason: a finding the inventory does not describe is a finding nobody was told about, and an inventory entry the checker cannot reach is a promise nobody keeps. This file is NOT harness/rules.json: that inventory is the contract rules in cafaye_contract.py, and an account-scope finding in there would break the assertion that the two sets are the same set.
notEnforced: `app.route("/v1", v1())` IS READ AS axum's `.route(path, handler)`, so a Hono sub-application mount becomes an `undeclared` finding against `/v1`. MEASURED on `harness/tests/fixtures/account-scope/hono_composed`: exactly that, at src/index.ts:24, and 0 occurrences in the fleet's seven services — the only other `.route(` in the fleet is Playwright's `page.route` in two e2e specs, which no `surface.sources` names. A real and separate defect, left in the fixture rather than written around, and recorded in `REPORT-core-hono-inline-01.md` §5.

A WILDCARD THIS CHECKER CANNOT EVALUATE. `mount_covers` decides `*`, a trailing `/*` and the exact path, and returns `(False, False)` — not covered AND NOT DECIDED — for anything else, because reading an unevaluated pattern as "does not cover" is how a `use` that matches nothing becomes the gate for every route in a file. MEASURED: 0 occurrences in the fleet, where both of guard's wildcard mounts spell it as a bare `*` or a trailing `/*`. The gap is theoretical today and the fallback is the loud one.

A MOUNT WHOSE PATH IS NOT A STRING LITERAL. `app.use(ROUTE_MOUNT, proxy)` passes a constant, and reading its value is the same second resolution this file does not make anywhere else. MEASURED on this fleet: 1 of guard's 4 `app.use` registrations, at src/index.ts:207, where `ROUTE_MOUNT = "/v1/*"` is declared in src/routes/table.ts:85. It is neither credited as a gate nor treated as a barrier, so `scoping-bypassed` still fires on a route behind it — the LOUD direction, which is the one this file prefers over silence, and one row in the whole fleet.

A CHAIN THAT LEFT THE FILE. `api.use("/*", accountGate)` names a middleware defined in another module, so what it does is not in the file the route is registered in and the checker cannot follow it. MEASURED on `harness/tests/fixtures/account-scope/hono_composed`: 1 of that fixture's 2 mounts, and 0 occurrences in the fleet's seven services today. The route is NOT called unscoped — `Recogniser.carries_handler`'s own refusal, restated for a chain this checker cannot read — and there is also no warning, so the row is silent in both directions. That gap is [D45]](../DECISIONS.md#d45-should-a-chain-the-checker-cannot-follow-say-so-or-be-silent), and it is the price of not firing on a correct route.

A handler dispatched as a property of an object the checker cannot resolve. MEASURED, not guessed: guard's `app.post("/auth/login", bff.requireSameOrigin, bff.login)` scores 1 of 5 on the real repository — the inline `/v1/me` route is caught on its registration line and the four `bff.*` routes are not, because resolving `bff.login` means resolving the type of the receiver `bff`, which is a second resolution this file does not make. That is 4 false negatives on one repository and it is recorded here rather than papered over by broadening the signal until it fires on things it cannot justify.

Whether an `accountScoped: false` row is a LIE about a database rather than a route. This file reads the route's account, never the query behind it. A route that resolves an account and then does not use it is a defect `tenancy.yml`'s `entryPoints` and harness/tenancy_check.py decide, and the reason those two files exist rather than one.

A route in a framework syntax the six RECOGNISERS do not know. Measured on this fleet: chi, chi-1.22, Phoenix, Hono/Express, Next.js App Router and axum are recognised; a Rails `config/routes.rb` is INVISIBLE and never becomes `undeclared`. If the declaration kept its row, that row's `registeredAt` line no longer registers the route and `account-scope.registration-commented` or `account-scope.stale` fires — but only because the row SURVIVED the refactor, which is not something a checker can rely on.

THAT A ROW EXISTS FOR EVERY REGISTRATION, which is the whole of what `surface.minimum` is for and the reason it is not a duplicate of the per-row findings. `stale` and `registration-commented` are both per-ROW: they ask whether a row the declaration still has points at a line that registers it. A route deleted together with its own row therefore leaves nothing for either to be stale about, and the count is all that is left — MEASURED on the conforming fixture with the `/healthz` registration and its row both removed and `get-message` re-pointed: `surface-thin` is the only finding, and lowering `minimum` by one turns it green. So the floor catches a shape no per-row check can express, and it is also a number in the file that went stale, which is why lowering it needs a reason rather than a keystroke. Neither number nor check is sufficient alone: with the per-row check a route deleted WITH its row is invisible, and without it a route deleted while its row stayed is invisible.

A route registered in a file `surface.sources` does not name. This is the honest cost of a declared surface: the enumeration is the authority and the sources are only where `undeclared` is decided. A service that names the wrong file has a checker that reports a clean answer over the file it did not read.

A scope prefix. `/v1/webhook_endpoints` and `/webhook_endpoints` both resolve to Phoenix's `get "/webhook_endpoints"`, because resolving `scope`/`mount` nesting is the guessing that produced three different answers across five repositories. A declared path is therefore a suffix match and the prefix is never verified.

Whether the reason on an `accountScoped: true` entry point is the RIGHT reason among the true ones. The contradiction check decides `false` against the code; nothing decides that a scoped route was scoped the way its reason says.
The method inside a method list. An `ANY` declaration matches any verb, and a framework registration written as `route("/x", get(h))` is read as GET from the handler position only.

Any tenancy key but four spellings. KEY_SPELLINGS is `account_id`, `accountId`, `accountID` and `account-id`, measured across identity, courier and guard; a service that names the column `tenant` passes this check and finds nothing here. The contradiction check does NOT depend on that list — it looks for the account being RESOLVED rather than for a key name — which is why it fires on `conn.assigns.current_account` and would fire on `tenant_id` too, though its `tenant` spellings are the least measured part of it.

Whether an entry point's account-scoped HANDLER actually scopes. This file proves the declaration still describes the tree. Whether the statements behind the handler scope their rows is tenancy.yml's `entryPoints` and harness/tenancy_check.py, which is why the two files exist rather than one.

Block structure written without indentation. `pipeline_evidence` finds a `do` block as the lines indented at least as far as the line that opened it, because Elixir has no braces. A Phoenix router that does not indent its blocks is a router this cannot read, and the rows behind it report `contradiction-unreadable` rather than passing silently.

findings.claim: a declared account-scoped entry point names the line that resolves the caller's account, and that line no longer carries the account key. The route was scoped and is not, and this is the only version of a cross-tenant read a declaration can catch on its own.
findings.remediate: put the account back on that line, or move `accountFrom` to the line that does resolve it — and if the route genuinely stopped being account-scoped, change `accountScoped` to `false` with a reason rather than leaving the row

findings.claim: an entry point declared `accountScoped: false` whose handler or account-resolving middleware this checker could not resolve to a file on disk, so no evidence could be sought or ruled out. Silence here is not a pass: the row was not verified, and it was not verified for a reason.
findings.remediate: name the router's middleware and controller modules the way this repository already spells them, and if a module is in another repository say so in a comment on the row — a checker that cannot resolve a symbol says so rather than trusting the declaration

findings.claim: an entry point declared `accountScoped: false` reaches another account's data: the request carries an account that was resolved on the caller's credential, or the handler reads one, or the handler lets the caller NAME one. The enumeration was complete and the answers were false, which is the D18 defect in the one form the omission check cannot see — a checker that asks `did the author enumerate their surface?` is answered yes by a declaration that lies.
findings.remediate: change `accountScoped` to `true` and name the line the evidence is on in `accountFrom` — or, if the route really is not account-scoped, remove what the evidence names, because the finding prints the file and line it found

findings.claim: the service reaches customer data and declares no account-scoped entry point, so which of its routes reach another account's rows is a question about route syntax.
findings.remediate: write account_scope.yml; the format is documented in docs/account-scope.md and the schema is schemas/account-scope.schema.json

findings.claim: account_scope.yml is not a YAML document core's reader accepts.
findings.remediate: run: harness/bin/account-scope-check <repo> --explain, and read the file and line it names

findings.claim: two declared entry points share an `id`, so a reader, a test and a failure message all name the same thing for two different routes.
findings.remediate: give each one its own id — `uniqueItems` cannot catch this because two rows that differ only in `line` are two objects

findings.claim: the service enumerated its surface and not one entry point on it is `accountScoped: true`. Either the enumeration is short of the truth or the answer is that this service reaches no customer data, and only one of those is a decision.
findings.remediate: check the routes that read a customer row and are declared `false`; a service that holds other people's data and says so nowhere is the D18 defect in a form a checker can now see
run: harness/bin/account-scope-check <repo>, and fix the keys it names — an undeclared key is a silent no-op everywhere else

findings.claim: the line a declaration row points at still NAMES the route and every mention of it is inside a comment, so the entry point is not mounted. This is not `undeclared` and it is not `stale`, and it is a failure rather than a warning because it is the one shape where the declaration and the file agree about a route that does not exist: a refactor commented the registration out, left the row, and the file still prints `r.Get("/healthz", handleHealthz)` on the exact line `registeredAt` names. A reader skimming the file believes it as readily as the checker used to, so a checker that reads the comment and moves on reports a deleted route as a mounted one with a file and a line and exits 0.
findings.remediate: make that line register the route again — uncomment it, or delete the row if the entry point really is gone, and NOT by pointing `registeredAt` somewhere else: this line names the route and registers nothing, so there is no such line

findings.claim: nothing in this repository names the tenancy key, so the account lines were searched for in four spellings this checker chose rather than one the service declared. A service whose key is spelled `tenant` passes every check here.
findings.remediate: declare `scope.key` in tenancy.yml — the checker reads it and searches for that — or in this file's own `surface.accountKey`, which is what the field is for

findings.claim: an entry point declared account-scoped names the function that resolves the caller's account, and the line registering the route does not go through it. The route was scoped and is not, with `accountFrom` still pointing at a middleware that nothing calls — which is the whole reason the declaration names the symbol rather than only a line.
findings.remediate: put `via` back on the registration, or change `accountScoped` to `false` with a reason — leaving a row that says a route is scoped when it is not is worse than having no file, because the file is what a reader trusts

findings.claim: this file and `tenancy.yml` name two different services, so the two declarations of one repository disagree about which repository they are about.
findings.remediate: make `service` agree, or delete whichever file is in the wrong repository — two files naming two services is a copy somebody made and nobody checked

findings.claim: a declared entry point is no longer registered where the declaration says it is: the route was renamed, or its registration moved, or the file no longer holds it.
findings.remediate: update `registeredAt` to the line the route is registered on, or delete the row if the entry point is gone — line numbers do not participate in identity, so a refactor that moved it three lines down is the only thing this is for

findings.claim: the service declares entry points and names no file in which they are registered, so nothing can be checked against the enumeration. This is the D18 defect with the word `undeclared` attached: a surface nobody read.
findings.remediate: name the router file(s) under `surface.sources` — one file rather than a directory wherever the repository allows it, because `surface.minimum` counts what is in it

findings.claim: a file named in `surface.sources` is not in this repository, so the declaration points the checker at something that is not there and `undeclared` cannot be decided against it.
findings.remediate: fix the path, or drop it — a source that is read as itself and does not exist is a checker looking at nothing

findings.claim: fewer entry-point registrations are in the declared sources than `surface.minimum` says there should be, so the surface has shrunk since the floor was set.
findings.remediate: read the diff that made it shrink and lower `minimum` to the number that is true now, with the reason in a comment — the floor exists to catch a route that moved into a file the checker cannot read, so lowering it needs a reason rather than a keystroke

findings.claim: a registration is in a file `surface.sources` names and no row of the declaration covers it. This is the finding the file exists to produce: an entry point nobody declared is an entry point nobody reviewed.
findings.remediate: add a row for it — `accountScoped: true` with `accountFrom`, or `accountScoped: false` with a `reason` — or move it out of the declared surface if it is a test's route table
